blocks.x: Eddie Dawson. Is that your full name? That's my full name. Eddie J. Dawson. Joseph Dawson. Eddie Joseph Dawson. Okay, and today is April the 5th. April the 5th, yes.

And it's 1972. 1972. Just beginning. Yeah, my name's Dick Allen. Let's get everybody's name then. Norse Edigo. Osberg. And that's spelled A with a little O over it. Yes, yes. C-E-R-G. Osberg. I'm trying to pronounce it right. Yeah, that's right. I have a hard time with these Swedish names. I know, yeah. What I wanted to ask you about was some of these people, you know, that, that nobody, uh, might remember very much about, like, did you know, uh, Babu, I'm sorry, Bubu Valentin? He played the valve trombone, and he repaired shoes. They also called him Bubu Augustin. No, I can't remember. Uh-huh. I can't remember. Oh, and can you tell me a little bit about St. Catharines Hall? Didn't you live there?

Yeah, St. Catharines Hall was, uh, on Tulane Avenue near Howard. Uh-huh. Yeah, I was, uh, altar boy. I used to be altar boy, you know. And I was raised up in the Third Ward, you know. And, uh, I attended, I used to, I just, I went to school at St. Catharines Church. Oh, they had a school, and a church, and a hall? Yeah, they had a school. And a hall? A church and a hall, a school in the back. Uh-huh. And where did the people dance? We never had no dance there, now that's in Catharines. Oh, I thought, they had, they had a hall around the corner. Oh, I see. They had a hall around the corner from the, from the church. Uh-huh. Uh, and that's where they used to have entertainment, you know, at the hall. Well, whose hall was it? Did it? That's St. Catharines. It belonged to St. Catharines. Oh, I see.
Because it was in the church, yeah. Yeah. And who would play in there?

Well, different bands, you know, like, I played with Rene there, kid Rene played there. We played there many times there, St. Catharines Hall. I remember now. And, uh, I believe, uh, I don't know where Buddy played, uh, but I know they had different bands that used to play there. Whose Buddy? It's been so long, Buddy Petit, you know. Oh, yeah. They had so many different bands. At that time, they had Kid, uh, Howard, and they had, uh, uh, Chris Kelly. Chris Kelly's band. And they had, uh, the, uh, Pelican band with, uh, Edwell Clem, the leader, and, uh, Frankie Duesen trombone. Oh, I remember? That was the Pelican band. Uh, then, uh, uh, uh, uh, the trombone player, they, uh, uh, oh, he's away now, the old trombone player. He played, uh, he played, uh, he was, uh, from, uh, Rampadita and Liberty. Uh, I'm trying, I'm trying to think of his name now. When did he leave town? He's been gone away, oh, 25, 30 years. Did he leave before Kid Ory, or after? Oh, Ory. That's the fella. Now, Ory, Ory was, uh, he was around, he lived around Padida and Liberty, around Padida and Liberty, around there. Uh, uh, and he used to play, uh, spot jobs with Frankie Dues, with, with Edward Clem on the trombone. He was, then after that, Ory formed his own band. Uh, uh, he formed his own band and, uh, he left and went away. He's been gone ever since.
Mm-hmm. What, that, St. Catherine Hall, did they have, uh, dances there every night or just on the weekend?
No, once a week like that, once a month like that. Oh, yeah. The Catholic place, you know. Oh, yeah. And, uh, they used to give, uh,
He was open to the public like anybody could go there. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

They sell tickets or? Yeah, sell tickets, yeah. They had a, had a music stand and everything in the back of the big hall. They served liquor in that? No, no liquor, no. That priest, Father Moe, he was, Father Moe was the,
Would you all like a Coke to drink? Oh, yeah. Yeah, go ahead.
Father Moe was a Catholic, uh, was a priest. He had, uh, he had charge of that, of the church and the hall.
Would they have something, something, something like food or anything like that?
Oh, like sandwiches and soft drinks, like, no liquor, though. I couldn't hear you for that truck. What did they have? Soft drinks and sandwiches. That's all.
Were the people, was it the priest allowed the people to, to, uh, dance?

They had to buy, buy stuff. Yeah, they allowed, he allowed them to dance in the hall, you know. Oh, but they didn't dance right here in the hall. No, no, no, no. There wasn't no ratty dancing at that time.
Did they play Get Out of Here? At midnight or anything like that?

Well, they played most of all the Dixieland jazz music like we play now, yeah. Did they play hymns too? Yeah, yeah, now and then they played hymns, yeah. You see, all that Dixieland jazz music we play now, that's when it come up from that time, it started.
We started that way. Oh, who was the band playing there when you were an altar boy? Did they have a band in the hall there?

Well, they had different bands used to play there, and, uh, but at that time I wasn't in, uh, I, I wasn't playing no music. Uh-huh. I was just going to school, you see, and I was a member of that church, you see, and by going to the school there, I began, uh, they made me altar boy. See, I was a Catholic before I joined all the Masonic organizations. After I joined each fraternal organization, I had to change my religion. So, I got into, uh, to Prince Hall Masons, Oddfellas Lodge. Well, you're a Colonel now, aren't you, at least? Yeah, I'm Colonel of the 13th Regiment of the Grand United Order of Oddfellas. Mm-hmm. That's, uh, Military Department of the Oddfellas. Mm-hmm. The ones you see that makes them parades in the street. Yeah. Well, how high can you get up? Can you get to be a General? You can be, you can be a, you can be a General, get as high as a General, and Brigadier General. Mm-hmm. You get to be a Brigadier General. Now, right now, I'm a Colonel and also a Major on the Grand Staff of the Paper Guard. Mm-hmm. See, the Grand Staff meets in, uh, Gary, Indiana, in August. Mm-hmm. You're going up there now? I got to go. I got to go. I'm a Grand Staff Officer. Mm-hmm. I got to go. I got to bring in my report. See, I have, uh, uh, you have to have so many companies to have a, to have a staff. That's how I got the staff of the 13th Regiment, but I have them by four, five different companies here, you see. Yeah. And I have a company, uh, 166 in Gullport. And I got 150 in, uh, in Amesville, Marrera, over there in, in Amesville, across the river. Mm-hmm. And, uh, on this side, in Yarlene's side, we got 150, Patriarchy 150, and Patriarchy 118. And then I got, uh, three daughters, auxiliary daughters. Number seven daughters. Thank you. One 18 daughters. And, uh, 166 from Gulfport. Oh, four 18. Mm-hmm.

Pass one on. Okay. Here, no. One, one. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. I need you up already. Yeah, I'm good. Okay, thank you. Yeah. Yeah, so, uh, let's stop here for a minute and check if it's recording okay. Mm-hmm. We were talking about the oddballs and you were telling about even as far as Gulfport, you got the daughters.

Yeah, that's all jewelry daughters of the military department. Mm-hmm. That keep you pretty busy, all that? Yeah, when we make parades, you see, we turn out twice a year, uh, for Peter Ogden Day and Patriarchy Memorial. That's, uh, in October. When is Peter Ogden Day? That's on, uh, Sunday in, uh, May.
Well, why did they choose the second Sunday?

Because the, uh, the Grand Lodge was meeting on the first Sunday. They used to meet on the first Sunday, coming in, contract, uh, contacting with the Grand Lodge and then they changed it. They had to change it.
Oh, I thought it was, was, is it doing anything to do with Peter Ogden's birthday or anything?
Peter Ogden's anniversary, yeah.
When was he born?
Oh, uh, you know, it's been so long now. Yeah.
So, uh, Flo, do you have the history of Peter Ogden? Ain't you got a, eighteen? Was he born on the 10th of May or something?
Uh, he was, uh, I think he was born in, uh, in that month.
Because they used to have, yeah, they used to have, uh, parades on that day.
Yeah, every, every year they were celebrating for, uh, his anniversary around, on, around the second Sunday in May.
And you've been going to those parades for a number of years?
Oh, yeah.
How long did you been there on from him?
Well, since, uh, 1920. Mm.
Mm. Mm. Mm. 1920, that's a long time. Well, he was a grown man in 1920, didn't he? Yeah. Yeah. Triumph. What about, who is the oldest oddfella in town?
Uh, well, uh, you know Booker T? Mm-hmm. Booker T's the old, uh, boy. Booker T's the old, uh, boy. Booker T's the old, uh, boy. That drum player.
He's older than you.
He's older than you.
Yeah. He's 90. Yeah, you know him when you were a little boy?
Yeah, I know him for years, boy. He's older than you. Yeah.
Did you ever play with him?
Oh, yeah. We played with him. You see, Booker T used to play in a, uh, regularly entertaining band, you know? Yeah. Dance band. Sit down? Yeah. He used to play that-a-way.
Double drums or single drums?
Yeah, snare and bass drums together. Yeah. Yeah. Like all the rest of them played. He was a good one.
Why did he stop playing?
Well, he took up with the brass band.
Well, he think he could do better than it. Mm-hmm.

He got so famous on the-in the brass band, in the marching band, you know? See, he stopped. He really-he really can play a good bass drum, you know? Yeah. Mm-hmm. Listen, them bass drum players are hard-a-good ones, you know? They hard to find.
So he-he used to be a good regular drummer?
Oh, yeah. He's a good drummer.
Was he a grown man when you were a little boy? Oh, yeah.
He was-well, he was, uh, uh, a young man, you know? Uh-huh.
So he's-

About ten, ten, ten years or so, more, older than me, you know? Mm-hmm. He had to be younger than me, because he's older than me. Mm-hmm. What band did he play with that you remember? Let's see, well, I think it was the Exceltia band. It used to have-they had the-they had the Exceltia band, uh, brass band.
They had the Eureka, they had the Olympia, and the Arnold, to my knowing, that's about the oldest band, you know, brass band, marching band.
Now, I mean, you said he was playing regular drums, uh-and-
Now, I mean you said he was playing regular drums.

Well he was playing with, just like I said, the Eureka, they had the dancing band, they had the Eureka, Excelsior, you had the Peron's band, you had the Body Petit, and the Creole Serenade, Peter Bokaz's band, and Celestan, I just can't think of all the names of the different bands.
You mean he played with all of those bands?

No, he didn't play with all of them, he only played with the Creole band from downtown, CD from downtown. That's what we played with. Yeah, most musicians like that, they cater to right in the area where they're from. See, like musicians would live downtown, they catered more to the downtown band, and the ones that live uptown, uptown band.
So who specials, do you remember, anybody specials that he played with? You talk about Creole band?

I wouldn't, no, I can't think, that's been so long. Well, we can ask him, he might ask. Yeah, he'll tell you, he can tell you. Can you interview him? He'll give you, he can give you a good idea. He'll do it again, though. Mm-hmm. Want to go back and see him again? Who was in the Pelican band, other than Stalin, Frank?
Edward Clem, who was the trumpet player, the leader.
Willie Warner was the clarinetist. Franky Dooson, who was the trombone player.
Mm-hmm. Um. .
I think the fella's name now on the drum, a little dog fella. Just can't think of his name right now. But I know I was, Bob Lyons was playing bass and I was playing guitar.
So you started on this guitar playing?
And after Bob Lyons and Edward Clem had a falling out, Edward put me on the bass.
Oh, I see.
That's where I started, Clem.
Well, who played the guitar then?
Uh, he got, uh, they had, uh, Emile O'Reilly.
Oh, Emile O'Reilly?

Emile O'Reilly played. Often on, they didn't have, you know, they had different guitar players. Sometimes he couldn't have a regular guitar player. After you know, they played, they didn't be playing spot jobs would it, you know? Yeah. But they had, he used Emile O'Reilly most of the time. Now that was a band that was a country band. That band was more out of town than it was in town. They'd take all up the road, up there, around Emile. Uh, Lacombe, Viola Combe, Viola Fush, Lake Charles, Shreesport. We just lived on the road. And, uh, that time they had the Southern SP train running.
Uh-huh.

And Edward Clem had a, uh, uh, uh, Jake, a good pull with the conductor. Uh-huh. And he would just bring us all up, right, and tell the conductor that we was his band, and we didn't have to pay. He had a certain amount of price he paid for us, you see? Oh, he got a whole lot of money. And they would put tickets. When we'd get on the train, they'd make all the bands sit in one place, and put a little strip of tickets on your hat, just in your cap. That's so they'd recognize you.
Did you play on the train ever?

No, we never played on the train. We just had, uh, we kept, we, we'd go right on to the destination where we had to get off. Sometime we'd play in, in, in, uh, Viola Fush. Sometime we'd be over there for two, three nights, you see. Yeah. Had a weekend like that.
Where was he from, Clem?

He was, he was, this is his home here in Yardines, but, uh, he's, he came from up in the country somewhere, but I never did find out. But he, uh, he lived here all the, and the time I started with him, you know.
And who did you say the drummer was?
Uh, I don't know if he didn't even, uh, uh.
Well, who did he play with?
He, he, uh, all I knew him, he never did play with no other band, but he, he was a good little drummer. He's from uptown.
Uh. Not, well let me name some drummer, see if you know him. D.D. Channel was from uptown, huh? No. Mac Murray? No. Uh, Willigans? No. Wasn't that guy named Tillman?
Tillman, no, wasn't Tillman.
Uh. You're kind of running out of uptown drummer from uptown. Uh, hmm.
He was a good little drummer, little dark fella. I hadn't named the other day I was thinking about it. Not Lacey.
Uh. No. Not little Mac Lacey. No. My little Mac Lacey. No.
Now there was one drummer that, that, that he used it most of the time. I think it was, he used this drummer more than he did any of them. The one, they had a boy they called Cook Shop Son.
Oh yeah, I heard him.

He was, uh, he was the first drummer played with, uh, Edward Clinton. Yeah, his mama had a cook shop. His mama had a cook shop on, on, was it Frank, Liberty Street, Max Liberty, Saratoga. By Rischak? About a school. You know where that Arthur Williams School was? Uh-huh. Right in the middle of the block. That's why we called him Cook Shop Son. But every time we needed him we had to go by the cook shop and get him in.
Yeah, well let's see, where was Henry Martin from?

Henry Martin was right across the street at the Arthur Williams School. Yeah, he was right there. Yeah, he, they came to, all the Martin brothers came up from that school. See, Henry Martin, Kutcher Martin, Don, Don Martin. Who was Don?
John Martin was a bass player.
Oh, I don't know a thing about him.
No? Who did he play with?
Well, he just, well, he played, didn't have no local band. We just used to go out and serenade at nights like that. Oh, yeah?

Well, I know a guy named Don Martin, but he's a cartoonist for Mad Magazine. He loves jazz, too. He took a beautiful picture of Mealy Barnes. You ought to see that picture. Yeah. Oh, gosh, yeah. Yeah. Don Martin was a bass player from the Orleans?
Yeah, he was, he was a little amateur bass player. Yeah. You see, he started on the guitar, you know.
All guy, but there you go. Yeah.
And he put the guitar down and took up the bass. It was a little, four, five piece band, you know, that's all it was.
Did you serenade much?

Oh, yeah. That's what I started with. When you guitar, huh? Yeah, going out at night parties on Saturday night, weekend, good timing. I used to play mandolin, too, you know. Yeah, I know. Started on the mandolin. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Did you play banjo also?
Mandolin, guitar, and bass.
Did you play banjo also?
Banjo, no, I wasn't playing no banjo then. I only took up banjo after I started with Hippolyte Charles.
What about your sister Anna? Did she play music?
No, she couldn't play no music at all. But she liked music, didn't you?
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah, I think, yeah. Musicians? Did she like musicians?
Yeah, but she, uh, uh.
Eddie Garland told me he used to go out with us, is that right?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, that was his old girlfriend. Yeah. Yeah, Eddie Garland, that's my sister Anna, yeah, that was her boy.
How old do you think Eddie Garland is? He's much older than you.
Oh, he's around eighty. He should be around eighty. He's, uh.
He's younger than you?

Oh, yeah, he's younger than me. Yeah. You see, at that time when, uh, when Eddie Garland, he, he, he was a member of his brother's band, Johnny Garland. Johnny Garland was a clarinet player. He's brother, he's brother of the clarinet. Now he, he had a band, he had a six-piece band, from uptown, see. Uh-huh. Now Eddie Garland, he couldn't, he couldn't pick, pick the bass, you know, he didn't know much about that. But playing with a bow. Yeah, he was good.
He was good with a bow.
Well, who did? In fact, I, I'm the one who started that four-four rhythm with one thing. Uh-huh. You used to play with a bow too? Yeah. I was my main out with a bow. Yeah.
I, I still got my bow, yeah, too. Yeah.

Yeah. When did you, when did you change from playing bow to picking? Well, uh, you see, we, uh, the, we used to play a variety of music. We had class, we, we used to play class music, then we played Dixieland, you see. And there's certain pieces we played, it called for a bow, you see. Like, there was some, uh, sentimental pieces like that to me. And, uh, we used to have to use the bow. But, uh, all this Dixieland and jazz stuff, you play that good with a, with a bow. Uh, we had one fellow who was the bass, greatest bass player we ever had. I don't know, he died, a fella called Pickaninny.
I never heard of him.
Oh, you talk about a bass player, whoo!
He played with a bow?
Man, he, no, he played, he played with a bow, and he could pick too.
Yeah.
Yeah, but man, he couldn't, he couldn't master that bow too. Uh-huh. He could make all them double wraps and everything on the, on the bass.
Did you know Chicken, Banks?
Chicken, Arthur Blanks. Yeah. Arthur Banks. Yeah, what did he play? Manolin, Manolin Guitars.
Who did he play with?
Well, he didn't play with nobody. Just a little, good timing, good time on the weekend like that.
Of course I've never even played that little bit. Well, I don't remember. You probably worked on that reel, I didn't do that reel yet. Okay. Yeah, we, and uh, did the, Edward Clem ever use a violin?
He never, he used to use a violin, yeah, he had a violin. Mm-hmm. The, uh, had the old man from, uh, uh, Donisonville, Professor Young.
Mm.
He used to play violin.
See, these are all new names to me. Professor Young. I never, I never knew who he played with. I never knew who Pickin' Inny played with. Who did Pickin' Inny?
He didn't play with no man.
Pickin' Inny was just a paring name?
He just, uh, you could hire him though if the fellas would need a bass player. Mm-hmm. He'd go, he'd go play with you, you know, but he didn't, he didn't belong to no special band.
Well, he didn't, he wasn't, uh, he had another job in playing music.
He didn't, uh, he didn't, uh, he, I don't know what kind of work he done.
But I mean, he wasn't professional.

No, he didn't. But he was a good bass player though. Yeah. But most of the playing of Pickin' Inny would be with the little short band, you know, like, three pieces, four pieces like that. Yeah. That's the way he started with.
That were, do you think there was a lot of string bands when you, when you grew up, there was a lot of string bands, like mandolin guitar and bass and then?
Oh, short bands. Yeah, like that. Oh yeah, they had a white band from uptown had a five piece string band like that. Yeah. He used to serenade at night there.
Did you know the guys?
I know, but, uh, I, I've been so long that I forgot their names, you know.
Where did they live?
Live up in the Irish Channel, all around up there. Now, you know who could tell you, give you the history of them? Yeah. Raymond Boyk.
Oh, well, I'll ask you.
Raymond Boyk will give you the history of that white band.
Well, you know, the Shields used to be right up there. Yeah, well, they were.
I believe, uh, yeah. One of the Shields boys, I think, played mandolin.

Yeah. He and Buddy Bolden were buddies, come to think of it. They were good friends. See, the Shields were right in the neighborhood, so they knew all the, the Bolden games. Yeah. And you used to go around and play like with the string band like that? Yeah, yeah, yeah.

We serenade at night. We used to go around at people's friends' house. And, uh, we'd go around a friend's house and, uh, and, uh, surprise them. We'd get right by the door to Wendland. We'd, uh, we'd start playing the number, you know, and the people would, if they was in bed, they'd get up and leave us in, you know. And we'd start to get in little booze and drinks and things like that.
Did you use it to play dancing with a band like that too?

Well, we, uh, we could play it, you know, but it wasn't too much, you know. Most of the dancing people would hire bands. Music was so cheap at that time, you could get a band for three dollars and a half a man. Three dollars a man. Yeah. About seven or eight piece bands could play, you know, like, like the, uh, the Autocrat Club.
Yeah.
Yeah. Franz O'Veir, Santa's Senna's, all them clubs. You, uh, you could take eight, nine piece bands in there and make good music and they'd have big dances there.
Did you ever know anybody who played harmonica with those short bands?

Uh, let me see, there was, uh, I don't know, this fellow's name, uh, they'd have good harmonica played too. He played drum too. Uh, uh, trying to let me think of it now. Who he played with? Played with, uh, Kid Clayton. Oh, not Jacques. Uh, Bushy Head fellow, the, what's his name, what's your name, what's your name? Well, I used to know Jacques.
Jacques.
Jacques. Yeah.
Jacques.
He played bones too. Played bones and played harmonica. Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Well, yeah, Dave Bailey plays harmonica. Yeah, yeah. You know Dave Bailey?
Yeah, I know Dave Bailey, yeah. That's, uh, that was, uh, uh, uh, he, he played drum too, didn't he?
Yeah. Yeah.
Dave used to be with Chris, didn't he? Yeah, Dave, Dave, yeah.
George Lewis said he was at the best time of anybody.
From front, from front of town. Yeah. His brother played in the band.
Yeah, Duff Ernest, John.
Yeah, Duff Ernest played bass.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And what about you? Did you ever play harmonica? No.
I could play it, but I never thought about them. Hmm.
I just wondered, what about in those string bands? Who were some of the fiddle players?
Well, number one, Peter Boccage was a good violin player.
With the short bands?

No, he had a heavy band. Mm-hmm. But he was a good violin player. Mario Mineta was a good violin player. Uh, uh, uh, let's see, Freddie Kepard. Freddie, Freddie Kepard started on a violin when he started playing, before he took up trumpet. Mm-hmm. Uh, I see.
Well, did he play, um, like Peter, would he put you in the alley, or what?
He played all f***ing.
He could read music. Sight read.
Brady could?
Yeah. All those fellas.
I didn't know Brady could read.
All those fellas were good talent. They all could read music.
I thought he was an hour ago.

Yeah, but one man that I know that didn't get his learning, he got, he come up from the home, the generalist's home, but he didn't know the music, he know the notes, but I don't believe he knew much about Division.
Second side of real one, I just want to make sure. I see, yeah. You were talking about the guy who didn't know Division.
That was Louis Armstrong.
Yeah.
He got, he learned that when he went away. He learned how to read music after going away, but he wasn't no sight reader. He could spell a little, but not much.
What about somebody like Tinette? Do you remember Tinette?
Tinette, Tinette was a good musician. He was a violin player.
Yeah.
He was a violin player. He played, he worked with me at Harry Parker and Charlie Parker dance
Hall.

I was in 19, say 1920, at Fortify. And, uh, Manetto was on the piano and I was playing guitar. John Veen on the drum. And, uh, Tinette on the violin. We didn't have no trumpet, no. I had old man Willie Umprey on the clarinet. Uh-huh. Now, at that time, they didn't allow no, uh, blowing instruments in the district there. Oh, yeah. I'm the first man that put the blowing instruments there.
No brass, huh?
No brass was allowed in there.
What, he's got piano and drums?
Piano, drums, clarinet, guitar, you know. Wow.
Yeah.
They used to have, they had no bass.
They used to have your small band. Yeah.

Uh, well, you see, uh, they used to dance. They had, uh, they sell liquor there, you know, they had women working there, uh, hustling. And, uh, the fellas, people would come in there. Most of the men from off the ships, they'd come in there and spend money and dance. And go on and have a good time and put, uh, we had a kiddie box that we, that dropped the money in the kiddie box for the different numbers that they want to hear, you see. And, uh, now, uh, T-Net played, uh, the last I heard of him, he played with us. And, uh, he, uh, I don't know whether he died or what. Anyway, after the fire broke out by Billy Phillips around in the middle of the block, that, uh, that killed everything. everything. So I, by me, Freddie Cap had come through there with his cornet one night and the boss asked me to see if I could get him to play a piece. So I told him no, that it was against the law. We asked Freddie if he wanted to play a number with him. He told the boss man, Harry Parker, he said, I'll play if you protect me. So Harry Parker said, well, you don't have to worry. He said, you go ahead and play a piece with Eddie and I'll see you tomorrow. I'll go to the mayor and get a permit so you can play here every night. So he did that. And from that on, Hunts and Nagel way down at the next corner, Moraes, and he had, he got the Joe Oliver's band, a whole band. What was the reason for that? They figured it was too loud? Too loud, yeah. Disturbed the piece. The loudest instrument they had was a clarinet.

What about Abadese? Did you ever go by Abadese? Down there, I figured it was on the anvil. Well, it had another name and I can't remember. Something like the, the Princeton Inn or the Princeton Club or something like that. No, Joe Oliver used to be there with Big Eye Louie and Ernest Rogers and Wooden Joe was in there playing clarinet. Yeah. You know the place. That was the Magnolia band. No, I think Richard M. Jones was there. Not the Magnolia. Not the band that was on Hunts and Nagels, but another one. This is a four piece. Papa Selle's back. No, it's a four piece band with Joe

Olavon and Wooden Joe. Yeah, well, no, he had a whole band. Oh yeah, he had a whole band? Joe Oliver had a whole band. Mm-hm. Celestane. Joe Oliver had, he had Louis Kepard on the guitar, Pop Foster on the bass, and Willie Foster on the violin. That was Pop Foster's brother. And, uh, that's the, uh, the famous clarin, uh, clarinet and saxophone, uh, hot dog.

Oh yeah, Grace and Beauty. Maple Leaf, you know. Maple Leaf, yeah. Maple Leaf was popular too, yeah.
Black and White. I have a lot of that stuff. Yeah.
drummers? Bass class? Who were some of your favorite drummers? That'd be a good thing for you to know.

Now, Nanesh. Nanesh. Trepanyeh. Trepanyeh. That's my favorite drummer. He was better than Saeed. Saeed tell you that. Trepanyeh was another band who could read music, drum music. And he could tune his drum up, just like I'm telling you. Trepanyeh was a good drummer. He was what you call a clump. Anytime he sits in the band and two of them go, and I was a leader knockoff, Trepanyeh go on and whatever time he picked up. He's got that time. If you playing with him, he don't increase, and he don't decrease. He just play that certain time, until you knockoff. I don't care how many solos he take, he's gonna play the solo, they're gonna come right back at that same time. But see these fellas, they take a solo, when they come back, they're coming back like a circus, you see? That's increasing the time. Did he play solos? Oh yeah. Solos wasn't as great as they is now though. They're a bad buck, solos. Like they're doing now. Oh, let one fella take a solo, another fella take another. They play a number from the start of finishing, until they finish up. That's the way. It worked, huh? Yeah, it worked. That's what, yeah. There's no money. There's something late, they're starting with all them solos.
I get tired of it. Every band sounds alike, every number sounds alike to me. Don't miss it. They can't help it. They play the same thing.
Yeah. You come to Preservation, they play Tiger Rack, they play anything, they know what they play, you go right around the corner of Dixieland, they play the same thing.

I tried to get Pete to play, you know, the Entertainer and different Red Back numbers, from out of that book, and he wouldn't play them at Preservation. He was playing all this time. And everybody didn't understand why. But he didn't think he should play them at Preservation. Well, let's see what we got next. Uh, what were some of the best halls that you ever played in? I mean, for making good tips. You played in big halls here?

I never made no tips though. Only, only halls I made tips was, uh, was, uh, Hanson Nagel, and the Rays in Ivorville, Harry Parker, uh, Saratoga, uh, Saratoga and, uh, Ivorville. Billy Phillips was on, uh, Saratoga near the next corner of, uh, uh, uh, uh, more near Benville.

What about, did you ever go to Dixieland, ever play at Dixieland Hall in late years? No? You never played there? I thought maybe you'd make some tips. You know, I'm talking about where Cottrell and Papa French money, you never made tips there. No. No.

Well, it's funny. I would think that, you know, you'd make some good money at Jean Zami or Frantz Zami, but the band didn't get the tips? No, no, we, uh, we had a study, uh, uh, uh, stipulated price, you know. You're regular sound. They had a fixed, they had a fixed price, and the leader would charge them so much for the band. Uh-huh. And that's all. When we had so many hours to play, and that's all. When we start the playing, when it's time to knock off, we knock off, and they pay us off. No tips. There are people that tip you there. Yeah. What about the lakefront? Oh, now, lakefront. Now, Mama Lou, and, uh, the Happy Landing, them's the places where I was going to go. There are tons of places where I made tips there. Yeah. West End? Did you ever play out at West End? Yeah. Played at West End. Spanish Port and Millenburg. All the places. Yeah. I played out there with Tom Brown and them, and I'll tell you, this was Walter Preston and them. And you got tips there. Yeah, yeah. Short band. See, four pieces. What about Millenburg? Did you get tips there? Millenburg? No, I didn't make no tips. Every time I played Millenburg, I played with a heavy band, you know. And they just played for a straight,
Right, yeah, salary. That's all. Is Millenburg and Spanish Port and the West End changed much? Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Whew. See, I never saw them. Well, wine and water, you wouldn't know that place out there. Now, they used to have a dummy. They used to run from Decatur and the Lillusion Field. They used to have a little house there at the corner. Yeah. And that was the headquarters. Now that dummy would leave there, and she'd get loaded, and go on out to the Millenburg. See? Right on out to Millenburg. And that's where we had Veshaix and started from going out there to play, went through picnics and things out there we had. Fall asleep on the train, you told me. Oh, yeah. He fell asleep. And we was all out there waiting for him. And he got full of wine, full of liquor, and went to sleep on, had his heart on. And the dummy done went out there, and turned around, went back in town, and come back again. And we, we was looking for him, and the band said, Well, what are you? Let's go out there, see, and find out, and ask the conductor. And you see the fellow, musician down there, there's a fellow back there sitting, sleeping, in the seat there. He said he didn't brought him in town, brought him back again then. And they was basically laid up there when he was finding that thing. No. Yeah. Junk. But child had brought him back up there and washed his face and got him, got him straightened out there. And man, he blew up some stuff. Whew.
What about, uh, Tranchinas and, and the, uh, Tokyo Gardens and all those places in Spanish Fork? Were you ever out there?

Uh, no. Uh, only Tranchini that had a place where we played at with, uh, with, uh, Mumford ourselves. Uh, um, uh, Uh, let's see. Uh, he's king to the Mumford's too. He's a piano player. And, uh, the Tranchini had, he had a, he had a, all of them there at the corner of Claiborne and, and Tulane Avenue. Uh-huh. That was a nice spot there, but that was only for the weekend. Uh, Leon Mumford. Leon Mumford played trombone, uh, piano. Uh-huh. And I played, uh, I was playing banjo. And T-Boy Remy was playing trumpet. And, uh, uh, uh, what did we ever had on the drum? Uh, uh, I believe we had Erich Begau on the drum. Same show. Erich Begau was on the drum. We had about four or five pieces there.

Did you, did you know Henry Ponce? Ponce. Henry Ponce. He had a joint near Segretas. They had a little fight going. segments.chapter: Opening, St. Catharines Hall and the Odd Fellows
segments.title: Opening: names, date and Lars Edegran present
segments.summary: Dawson gives his full name; Allen states the date, 5 April 1972, and introduces the session and the people on his list.

segments.chapter: Opening, St. Catharines Hall and the Odd Fellows
segments.title: St. Catharines Hall and the bands that played there
segments.summary: Dawson describes the church, school and hall near Tulane Avenue where he was an altar boy, and lists bands that played there, including Kid Rene, Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly and the Pelican band, plus Kid Ory's early days.

segments.chapter: Opening, St. Catharines Hall and the Odd Fellows
segments.title: What dances at St. Catharines Hall were like
segments.summary: Dances were occasional, ticketed, with soft drinks and sandwiches but no liquor, under Father Moe; the bands played Dixieland and occasionally hymns.

segments.chapter: Opening, St. Catharines Hall and the Odd Fellows
segments.title: Catholic upbringing, the Odd Fellows regiment and Peter Ogden Day parades
segments.summary: Dawson explains he left the Catholic church when he joined fraternal orders, describes his rank in the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows military department and its parades, and says he has marched since 1920.

segments.chapter: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
segments.title: Booker T, the oldest Odd Fellow, from dance drummer to bass drum
segments.summary: Dawson recalls the drummer Booker T, about ninety, who played snare and bass drum in dance bands before becoming famous in the brass bands.

segments.chapter: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
segments.title: Brass bands and dance bands, downtown Creole and uptown
segments.summary: Dawson names the Excelsior, Eureka, Olympia and other brass and dance bands, and says musicians played with bands from their own part of town, downtown Creole or uptown.

segments.chapter: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
segments.title: Pelican band members and Dawson moving from guitar to bass
segments.summary: Dawson lists Edward Clem, Willie Warner and Frankie Dusen, says he played guitar with Bob Lyons on bass, and that after Clem and Lyons fell out he was put on bass; Emile O'Reilly took over guitar.

segments.chapter: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
segments.title: The Pelican band on the road by train in the country
segments.summary: The band worked mostly out of town, in Lacombe, Lake Charles, Shreveport and elsewhere, travelling by Southern Pacific train on a deal Clem had with the conductor.

segments.chapter: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
segments.title: Trying to name the Pelican band drummer, Cook Shop Son
segments.summary: Dawson cannot recall the drummer's name, an uptown man; Allen suggests drummers, and Dawson finally recalls the nickname Cook Shop Son because his mother kept a cook shop on Liberty Street.

segments.chapter: Booker T, the brass bands and the Pelican band
segments.title: The Martin brothers and Don Martin, amateur bass player
segments.summary: Henry Martin and the Martin brothers came from near Arthur Williams School; Don Martin, a little amateur bass player who started on guitar, played only serenades in a small band.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: Starting on mandolin and guitar, serenading, banjo with Hippolyte Charles
segments.summary: Dawson says he began with serenading on mandolin, guitar and bass, and only took up banjo after joining Hippolyte Charles.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: His sister Anna, Eddie Garland and Johnny Garland's band
segments.summary: Dawson's sister Anna did not play but liked musicians; Eddie Garland was her boyfriend, and played in his brother Johnny Garland's six-piece uptown band.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: Bowing versus picking the bass; the great bass player Pickaninny
segments.summary: Dawson says he started the four-four rhythm on bass, used a bow for sentimental pieces and plucked for Dixieland, and praises Pickaninny who did both.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: Chicken Banks, Professor Young and the freelance bass man
segments.summary: Dawson identifies Chicken (Arthur) Banks as a casual mandolin and guitar player, mentions Professor Young on violin with Clem, and explains Pickaninny played only short bands.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: String bands, a white band in the Irish Channel, and serenading
segments.summary: Short string bands were common, including a white five-piece band in the Irish Channel; Dawson describes surprising friends with night serenades for booze, and the Shields family's connection.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: What bands were paid for dances and clubs in the early days
segments.summary: String bands rarely played dances; dance hosts hired seven- or eight-piece bands for around three dollars to three-fifty a man at clubs like the Autocrat.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: Harmonica and bones players, Dave Bailey, and Dawson's own harmonica
segments.summary: Dawson tries to recall a harmonica and bones player who worked with Kid Clayton, talks about Dave Bailey and Duff Ernest, and says he could play harmonica but never did.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: Fiddle players: Peter Bocage, Manuel Manetta, Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: Dawson names Peter Bocage and others as good violinists, says Freddie Keppard started on violin, and that these men all read music at sight.

segments.chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
segments.title: Louis Armstrong learned to read music only after leaving
segments.summary: Asked about musicians who could not read, Dawson says Louis Armstrong came out of the home without reading and learned later, but was never a sight reader.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Playing at Harry Parker's in 1920 with Tinette and Keppard, and the brass ban
segments.summary: Dawson recounts a small band at Harry Parker's with Manetta, John Vigne and violinist Tinette; brass was banned in the district until Freddie Keppard played a number under Parker's protection.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Joe Oliver's band at Hunts and Nagel's, and a great clarinetist
segments.summary: Allen asks about Abadie's and other joints; Dawson says Joe Oliver had a full band with Louis Keppard, Pop Foster and Willie Foster, then tries to recall a clarinet and sax player who could read anything.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Playing guitar in Charlie Galloway's Dixieland band
segments.summary: Dawson played two or three years with bassist Charlie Galloway, who walked on a crutch, in a band with clarinetist Cripple Pill (Henry Ross).

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Guitarists and drummers Allen asks about: Mumford, Gibson, the Nixons
segments.summary: A run of quick questions about Brock Mumford, Frank Burnett, Hugh Rankin, Billy Peyton, Jim Gibson and the guitarist Philip Nixon and his brother Sam, a bass player.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: The Robert Charles riot and the Battlefield neighbourhood
segments.summary: Dawson recalls living on Bolivar Street and playing when the Robert Charles mob came, the Battlefield area and its tough men, and the old basin.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Policeman Bradley and the dice games on the Battlefield
segments.summary: Dawson tells how Bradley, a policeman, was beaten and disarmed by dice players; Allen asks about mounted officer Dutch Cromer.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: The two red-light districts and Black Benny's gang
segments.summary: Dawson describes the districts, around Franklin and Saratoga and near Basin Street, and the bad men Black Benny, Aaron Harris and Sawadick.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Tough women: Mary Jack the Bear and Ann Cook
segments.summary: Dawson says Mary Jack the Bear and Ann Cook were violent, recalls John Segretta's ballroom where Armstrong and Shots Madison played, and says he never knew Ann Cook as a singer.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: An organized band with a girl pianist, and Manuel Sales
segments.summary: Asked about female vocalists, Dawson describes a band with a woman pianist from St. Catharines, August Lanoix on tuba, T-Boy Remy and others, in which Manuel Sales later replaced him.

segments.chapter: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
segments.title: Did women in the district sing? Lessie, Esther Bijou and Lila Bolden
segments.summary: Dawson says the hustling women had talent but did not sing professionally; the two go back over Ann Cook, a violent woman called Lessie, and women who recorded.

segments.chapter: Draft, guitar and learning music
segments.title: Drafted for the First World War and the night of dime banks
segments.summary: Dawson was drafted but a letter after the armistice said he was not qualified; on the eve of leaving he serenaded all night and spent his dimes.

segments.chapter: Draft, guitar and learning music
segments.title: The Landry family and Tom Harris, who played with Galloway
segments.summary: Allen asks about the Landrys and Galloway band members; Dawson tangles over Tom Harris, Tom Alvin and guitarist Frank Landry.

segments.chapter: Draft, guitar and learning music
segments.title: Guitar finger-picking, embouchures and reading music
segments.summary: Dawson discusses Frank Landry's and Philip Nickerson's guitar styles, finger-picking and beats, the cornetist with his tongue showing, his two bass lessons, and his limited sight reading.

segments.chapter: Draft, guitar and learning music
segments.title: Teaching himself guitar from a method; rehearsals under Hippolyte Charles
segments.summary: Dawson learned guitar from a method book; good bands read and played by ear, rehearsal mattered, and Hippolyte Charles demanded it unpaid.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Camilla Todd, pianist with Hippolyte Charles, and where to find her
segments.summary: Dawson says Camilla Todd was a great pianist with Charles; the pair try to work out where she and her brother Clarence live, and suggest asking Sweet Emma.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Sorting out two violinists named McNeil
segments.summary: Allen and Dawson try to distinguish the McNeil who played at a Franklin Street dance hall from the one who played with Sonny Henry and Robichaux.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Sonny Henry and Albert Glenny in Hippolyte Charles's reading band
segments.summary: Dawson says Sonny Henry played in Charles's band and called him G7, Albert Glenny was on bass, and he himself played banjo reading parts the leader handed out.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Giving up banjo for bass with the Pelican band
segments.summary: After leaving Charles, Dawson joined the Pelican band, switched from banjo to bass when Bob Lyons and Clem fell out, and never went back.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Buying a bass on Rampart Street; the Palace Theater and Mama Lou's
segments.summary: He bought a cheap bass on Rampart Street, spent about four years at the Palace Theater in the Dejan band with drummers Pico and Dave Oxley, then played years at Mama Lou's with Andrew Jefferson.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Stale Bread, mandolin and banjo players, Tom Denton
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Stale Bread's white trio in the Irish Channel, rates Big Head Sun the best mandolinist, and says Tom Denton played banjo with the Pelican band.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Playing Scotch, French and German tunes; leading Joe Oliver's band on mandolin
segments.summary: Dawson talks about violin repertoire and quadrilles and cakewalks, and says he once led a seven-piece Joe Oliver band on mandolin at a lake picnic.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Jules Batiste, Johnny St. Cyr and playing with Robichaux
segments.summary: Dawson knew of Jules Batiste, praises guitarist Johnny St. Cyr, and says he played guitar in John Robichaux's full band before St. Cyr did.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Dawson's first mandolin, turtle shell and rosewood
segments.summary: Dawson shows Allen his old mandolin, his first instrument, which is inlaid with tortoise shell and ivory, and talk turns to an old photograph at age 23.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
segments.title: Tom Mitchell, trumpeter Mutt Carter and the Cashman brothers
segments.summary: Dawson plays through who Tom Mitchell played bass with, finally recalling the trumpeter Mutt Carter, whose band included John Cashman and Dawson on guitar.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Fish fry jobs for mandolin, guitar and bass trios
segments.summary: Willie Santiago and others played for pleasure, but trios earned two and a half to three dollars a man at private fish fries, where hosts also sold homebrew and bootleg.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Dawson on drinking, Jim Robinson and his father
segments.summary: Dawson says he still drinks, that a musician who can't drink is dead, and mentions his father drinking into his nineties.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Leaving the lumber yard for Canadian Jackson's band
segments.summary: Dawson says no one else in his family played; he left a lumber yard when Cornelius Jackson offered work, earned twenty-two dollars the first night, and later ran his own band at Harry Parker's.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Coochie Morton, his brothers and the line-up at Harry Parker's
segments.summary: Dawson describes Coochie Morton on guitar and his brothers, and his own band at Harry Parker's with Manetta on piano and John Vigne on drums.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Why they called him Rat: passing the hat
segments.summary: Dawson explains his nickname Rat, given by Alphonse Picou, because he was the one willing to pass the hat and could drop coins into his palm.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Gold from Norwegian sailors, diamonds, and women hustling for him
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Norwegian ships' gold coins, wearing diamond studs and cufflinks made of ten-dollar gold pieces, and living off women's earnings and his gambling.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Gambling games and women buying him pearl gray suits
segments.summary: Dawson played coon-can and poker, and describes women paying down on made-to-measure suits at Rampart Street tailors, as Manetta once did with Tony Jackson in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Fish fries, passing the hat and district living
segments.title: Emma Davis, long cuffs, Chicago flats and John B. Stetson hats
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Emma Davis bringing his supper while he played at Hunts and Nagel's, and describes the clothes of the time: cuffs, Chicago flats, Edwin Clapp shoes and Stetsons.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: The Big 25: Frank Keelan's fight and hitting a madam with a cue stick
segments.summary: Dawson tells of gambling at the Big 25, Big Zack beating Frank Keelan, and hitting a man with a cue stick who turned out to be a wealthy madam.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: Lewis Wade, Paul Gross and Buddy Bertrand around the Big 25
segments.summary: Dawson describes Lewis Wade as a pimp and pianist, Paul Gross as a gambler, and knowing pianist Buddy Bertrand only from the Big 25 district.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: Morphodites dressed as women in the district
segments.summary: Dawson explains that men dressed as women at night around the Big 25.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: King's ballroom, Oaky Pope and women hustling between districts
segments.summary: Dawson recalls the Italian ballroom owner King's place and its bartender Oaky Pope, and how groups of women moved from downtown to uptown hustling.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: Drugs in the district: pills, needles and opium pipes
segments.summary: Allen asks about pill rolling and cocaine; Dawson says dope was everywhere, with needles and opium pipes in the houses.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: George Jones and the Maestri patrons
segments.summary: Dawson played trios in the big houses for patrons like Maestri, and describes George Jones, a rhyming singer with a sash-cord bass who made money from improvised songs.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: The song about Maestri's furniture wagons
segments.summary: Dawson explains the song about Maestri's wagons repossessing furniture from people who could not pay.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: Rabbit Brown and the 'Spoonful' guitarist who hustled alone
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Rabbit Brown hustling without a band, and a guitar player singing Spoonful in barbershops and the French Market for tips.

segments.chapter: The district underworld and street musicians
segments.title: Walter Preston's band at Tom Anderson's, and the guitarist Snow
segments.summary: Walter Preston, Tom Brown, Charlie Washington and Snow played mandolin and guitars at Tom Anderson's and the halfway house; Dawson sometimes played bass, and the talk wanders into nose candy.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: His mother bought him a one-dollar guitar and he taught himself
segments.summary: Dawson tells how his mother bought an old guitar for a dollar from a player and he learned to tune and play it himself.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Chalky Banana learning from Kid Rene; musicians who steal licks
segments.summary: Dawson says Chalky Banana learned trumpet by following Rene's band, and that he hid his chord positions from fellows trying to steal them; Allen mentions 'alligators' and 'goats'.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Rene Batiste and the violinist Ferdinand Valteau
segments.summary: Dawson barely knew Rene Batiste and remembers old man Valteau as a good violinist who freelanced and never held a regular band job.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Lawn parties and Buddy Bowling's six-piece bands
segments.summary: Dawson describes backyard lawn parties with tarpaulins and lights, which paid well for bands like Buddy Bowling's.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Pelican band on the road; Robichaux's country band
segments.summary: Dawson says he played mostly with Dusen and Clem's Pelican band, on the road all week, and that Robichaux's reading band also toured the country.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Cutting the titles off the music to stop a copier at Hunts and Nagel's
segments.summary: At Hunts and Nagel's with Joe Oliver, a man copied titles of their third-grade sheet music, so Willie Foster had the titles cut off; Allen adds the 'Who Struck John' story.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Mama Lou's band with Andrew Jefferson, Al Fonce and Lionel Ferbos
segments.summary: Dawson recalls the Mama Lou's lineup around Andrew Jefferson, a leader with a full briefcase of music, trumpeters Al Fonce and Lionel Ferbos, and where to find them.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Musicians and barbershops
segments.summary: Dawson says few musicians cut hair, apart from Papa John, and that musicians did not hang around barbershops.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Jimmy Palao, sleeping Tinette, Keppard's prank and Willie Humphrey quitting
segments.summary: At Harry Parker's, Palao's substitute Tinette fell asleep playing and Freddie Keppard greased his bow; Willie Humphrey Sr. quit after a row with a beer hustler and George Baquet replaced him.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Solo players, violinists and the Lindsey family
segments.summary: Dawson says there were no solo players, repeats that Palao, Manetta and Bocage were fine sight-readers, and recalls the Lindsey bass player.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Uniformed dance bands and Hippolyte Charles's saxophone orchestra
segments.summary: Dawson describes the Olympia and Eureka dance bands in uniform, Hippolyte Charles's reading band with two saxes and a conservatory-trained leader, and the Blaze Away and Golden Rule bands.

segments.chapter: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
segments.title: Candy Dan, the Spoonful guitarist, and Lorenzo Staulz
segments.summary: Dawson finally recalls the Spoonful guitarist as Candy Dan, who hustled with a mandolinist across Canal Street; Allen asks about Lorenzo Staulz, and the tape is paused.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Whitney Bank
segments.title: Born in the French Quarter and moving uptown to Miro and Bolivar streets
segments.summary: Dawson was born downtown on Decatur between Esplanade and Barracks, attended a Catholic school until third grade, then the family moved uptown.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Whitney Bank
segments.title: His parents' languages and a trip to Belize
segments.summary: His mother spoke French and his father, William Dawson, a ship worker from British Honduras, Spanish; the family visited Belize for a month but left because of mosquitoes.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Whitney Bank
segments.title: Getting a night job at the Whitney Bank during work-or-fight
segments.summary: Dodging work-or-fight, Dawson got on the Whitney Bank night staff through a barbershop tip, arranged to leave for gigs, moved to a day job and worked fifty-two years until pensioned.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: No real teacher: help from Joe Welch and Manuel Manetta
segments.summary: Dawson says he taught himself but needed a teacher for note divisions, and got help from Joe Welch and Manetta.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Church jobs: St. Francis de Sales and sanctified churches
segments.summary: Dawson played in St. Francis de Sales later in life and earlier played guitar and mandolin for spiritual churches that sang, danced and beat tambourines, for a salary.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Sam Moran and Dawson on bass at Tom Anderson's with Frank Keelan
segments.summary: When bassist Sam Moran fell ill, Dawson took his place in Tom Brown's band at Tom Anderson's, with Frank Keelan on muted trumpet, mandolin, two guitars and no drum.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Early drummers: foot pedals, tuning drums and reading drum music
segments.summary: Dawson says drummers always had pedals, tuned their drums to a trumpet note, and few could read drum music, apart from Joe Welch.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Old-time cymbals, cow bells, ice cream bells, triangles and brushes
segments.summary: Dawson describes the percussion drummers used: small cymbals, cow bells, bell sets, iron triangles, and straw brushes for soft music.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Scott Joplin rags and the Red Back Book were hard to read
segments.summary: Dawson says playing Scott Joplin required real reading skill, and the two talk about Grace and Beauty, Maple Leaf and Allen's band.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Favorite drummer Ninesse Trepagnier; steady time and solos
segments.summary: Dawson names Trepagnier as his favorite drummer for his steady time and reading, and complains that today's solos make every band sound alike.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Which halls paid tips: Hunts and Nagel's, Mama Lou's, West End
segments.summary: Dawson says he made tips only at Hunts and Nagel's, Harry Parker's and the lakefront places with small bands; heavy-band dances were fixed price.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: The dummy train to Milneburg and the musician who slept through
segments.summary: Dawson describes the little train from Decatur to Milneburg, used for picnics, and a drunk musician who rode it back and forth asleep.

segments.chapter: Musicianship, drumming and the halls
segments.title: Tranchina's and Henry Ponce's joint
segments.summary: Dawson only played at Tranchina's at Claiborne and Tulane with Leon Mumford, T-Boy Remy and a drummer; Allen asks about Henry Ponce's joint near Segretta's.
